tagline: Prairie, wagon ruts and a river crossing along southern Nebraska.
intro: Heritage Highway follows US 136 for 238 miles between Edison and Brownville, close to Nebraska’s southern border. Nebraska’s Department of Transportation includes it among the state’s nine scenic two-lane byways. The Nebraska Tourism Commission promotes the route for its rivers, lakes, prairies, farmland and historic settlements, with communities preserving the state’s history across ten counties. At its eastern end, Brownville occupies the Loess Hills above the Missouri River Valley, where US 136 reaches its Nebraska crossing.

The highway’s Missouri River crossing began as a toll bridge built by Atchison County in 1939. In Nebraska, the road carried the Route 3 designation before US 136 replaced it in 1960. The Brownville crossing later became toll-free; its deck was replaced during repairs in 2009 and 2010.

Driving east from Edison brings you to Alma at the northwest end of Harlan County Reservoir, then to Willa Cather’s Red Cloud. Continue through Hebron and Fairbury, where Rock Creek Station preserves wagon-trail history, then toward Beatrice. Five miles west of Beatrice, Homestead National Historical Park includes some of the first acres successfully claimed under the Homestead Act. Beyond Auburn, the byway reaches Brownville on the Missouri; US 136 continues across the river on the truss bridge.

moments.title: Red Cloud
moments.text: Willa Cather’s childhood home is a clapboarded, wood-frame house just west of downtown Red Cloud. Her family moved into the rented house in spring 1885, and she lived there until leaving for college at seventeen. Red Cloud became a source for fictional towns, including Black Hawk in My Ántonia. Several nineteenth-century buildings described in her books belong to the Willa Cather Historic District. The Willa Cather Memorial and Educational Foundation bought the house in 1960 and oversaw its restoration to the period when Cather lived there. At the house, a porch spans the front beneath a shed roof, with decorative woodwork between square posts.
moments.notice: The childhood home’s front porch has square posts and a decorative woodwork valance.

moments.title: Rock Creek Station
moments.text: Deep wagon ruts remain at Rock Creek Station; the toll bridge and many station buildings are reconstructions. Established in 1857 on the Oregon and California trails, the station supplied emigrants and provided a campground. David and James McCanles bought the property in 1859 and added a toll bridge, charging wagons ten to fifty cents based on their ability to pay. The East Ranch later passed to the Pony Express owners on installment terms. In July 1861, James Butler Hickok killed David McCanles during an argument over an overdue payment. The Nebraska Game and Parks Commission began developing the state historical park in 1980.
moments.notice: Wagon ruts cut through the park’s prairie hilltops, creek bottoms and ravines.

moments.title: Brownville Bridge
moments.text: The Brownville Bridge carries US 136 across the Missouri River between Nebraska and Missouri. Atchison County built the bridge in 1939 for $700,000 and initially operated it as a toll crossing. HNTB designed it, and Bethlehem Steel built the superstructure. The cantilevered Warren through truss has a longest span of 419.8 feet. Repairs in 2009 and 2010 replaced the deck and repaired piers and steelwork. Flood damage to its approaches closed it for 216 days in 2019. The bridge entered the National Register of Historic Places in 1993; maintenance is now the Missouri Department of Transportation’s responsibility.
